title: Swift 6.2 — approachable concurrency
summary: A direct response to how hard Swift 6's strict checking was to adopt. Most of this release is about letting single-threaded code stay single-threaded without fighting the compiler, so you opt into parallelism rather than out of it.

changes.title: Modules can default to main-actor isolation
changes.detail: A build setting lets a whole module be implicitly @MainActor. For UI code — which is already main-thread-bound — this removes most of the annotation churn that Swift 6 introduced, because the isolation you already had is now the default rather than something you restate on every type.
changes.migration: Turn it on per target for app and UI modules. Leave it off for shared model or networking modules, where isolation should stay explicit.

changes.title: @concurrent marks the functions that actually leave the actor
changes.detail: Async functions no longer imply that they hop off the current actor. A function stays where it was called unless it is marked @concurrent, which makes the escape to a background thread visible at the declaration rather than inferred from context.
changes.migration: Mark genuinely parallel work @concurrent. If an async function only awaits other async work, it probably does not need it.

changes.title: Fewer Sendable annotations required
changes.detail: Improved inference means a great deal of code that Swift 6.0 demanded be annotated now checks out on its own. The underlying data-race rules did not loosen — the compiler simply got better at proving what you already meant.

title: Swift 6.0 — data races become compile errors
summary: The release the whole concurrency model was built toward. In Swift 6 language mode, code that could race is rejected at compile time rather than crashing intermittently in production.

changes.title: Swift 6 language mode enforces complete concurrency checking
changes.detail: Opt in per module. Sendable violations and cross-actor access that were warnings in Swift 5 mode become errors. This is the single largest source of migration work in a mature codebase, and it is deliberately opt-in per target so you can move one module at a time.
changes.migration: Enable complete concurrency checking in Swift 5 mode first and clear the warnings. Only then switch the module to Swift 6 mode.

changes.title: Typed throws
changes.detail: A function can declare the concrete error type it throws with `throws(MyError)`. Useful in constrained code and generic algorithms that need to propagate an error type precisely; ordinary application code is usually still better served by untyped throws.

title: iOS 17 — the Observation framework
summary: @Observable replaces ObservableObject for most SwiftUI state, and changes which views actually redraw.

changes.title: @Observable tracks property access instead of object change
changes.detail: With ObservableObject, any @Published change redrew every view observing the object. @Observable tracks which properties a view's body actually read, so a view only redraws when something it genuinely uses changes. This usually removes a whole class of over-rendering without any work beyond adopting the macro.
changes.migration: Replace ObservableObject + @Published with @Observable, and @StateObject/@ObservedObject with @State or a plain property.

changes.title: ObservableObject is now the legacy path
changes.detail: Still supported, but new code should not reach for it. It remains necessary only when deploying below iOS 17.

title: Swift 5.9 — macros and ownership
summary: Macros arrive as a first-class language feature, and the ownership model gains noncopyable types.

changes.title: Macros
changes.detail: Compile-time code generation with full type information. This is the mechanism behind @Observable and much of SwiftData, so understanding what a macro expands to is now part of reading ordinary framework code.

changes.title: Noncopyable types (~Copyable)
changes.detail: A type can declare that it must not be copied, giving the compiler enough information to enforce unique ownership of a resource. Relevant when a value represents something that genuinely cannot be duplicated, such as a file handle or a lock.

changes.title: if and switch as expressions
changes.detail: Both can now produce a value directly, which removes a great deal of `var x: T` followed by assignment in every branch.
